primary_diagnosis: NSAID-induced gastrointestinal bleeding with iron deficiency anemia and reactive thrombocytosis
clinical_reasoning_summary: The patient’s chronic NSAID use, persistent anemia, and marked thrombocytosis most plausibly reflect occult gastrointestinal blood loss leading to iron deficiency and a reactive platelet response. Metabolic syndrome is also likely given obesity, prediabetes, and borderline hypertension, though lipid data are missing. CKD, OSA, mitral valve sequelae, a primary hematologic disorder, mood disorder, and progression to diabetes remain possible but less certain. The reviewer’s probability adjustments and primary recommendation have been incorporated.
unresolved_findings: Elevated platelet count with high PDW – reactive vs primary cause not yet clarified
Mildly low hematocrit and low‑normal MCH – iron status unknown
Missing lipid panel (total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, triglycerides)
Missing renal function (creatinine, eGFR, urine ACR)
No imaging data on severity of mitral stenosis
Smoking, alcohol, physical activity, diet – not documented
Incomplete medication list (possible undocumented antihypertensives, statins, iron, PPIs)
recommended_workup: Serum iron studies (ferritin, iron, TIBC, transferrin saturation)
Fecal occult blood test and/or colonoscopy to evaluate occult GI bleeding
Renal function panel (serum creatinine, eGFR, urine albumin‑creatinine ratio)
Polysomnography for obstructive sleep apnea assessment
Transthoracic echocardiogram with Doppler to grade mitral stenosis severity
Medication reconciliation focusing on NSAID, antihypertensive, and iron supplement use
Referral to hematology for thrombocytosis work‑up (including JAK2 mutation testing) if iron deficiency is excluded
